related_content.relationship: A gi guard alternative organized around sleeve control and lasso/spider branches.

summary: A lapel grip alone does not provide the fabric length and access needed for a lapel-guard entry.
description: What Keenan Cornelius’s public lapel-denial discussion reveals about the setup a guard player needs.
overview: A guard player can hold a lapel and still lack enough loose fabric to form the intended entanglement. Jiu Jitsu X’s article featuring Keenan Cornelius explains that distinction from the passer’s side. It also covers approaches outside the legs and foot control, showing how a passer can obstruct the setup before a lapel guard develops.

guide.display_title: Lapel Guard: What Stops the Entry

fits: You obtain a lapel grip but struggle to establish the guard around it.

includes: Lapel slack and length as entry requirements.
Outside-the-legs approaches and foot control as obstacles to establishing lapel guard.
limits: The source focuses on denying entries. It does not provide a full worm- or squid-guard attacking curriculum.

sources.title: How To Pass Lapel Guards: Keenan Finally Comes Clean — Cristiano Del Giacco
sources.note: Read the public Jiu Jitsu X article presenting Keenan Cornelius’s lapel-denial concepts: available lapel slack, outside positioning and the calamari grip. Embedded demonstrations not reviewed.

flashcards.question: Does holding an opponent’s lapel alone establish a lapel-guard entry?
flashcards.answer: No. The Jiu Jitsu X article distinguishes having the grip from freeing enough lapel length to enter the position.
flashcards.answer_line: The grip also needs usable slack.
